messages.author: baa06f08a03a1251
messages.subject: Number of latent variables
parts:
Hello,
I have a naive question about model generation for GenomicSEM.

I have GWAS performed for 3 different biomarkers for a trait of interest.  Genetic Correlations for the three biomarkers are correlated (rg 0.3-0.6).

Each biomarker is determined by the trait and unique nontrait associated features.

Is it possible to perform Genomic SEM for 4 latent factors (as below) when I only have 3 traits, or is this model underspecified?

LatentTrait=~Biomarker1+Biomarker2+Biomarker3
Biomarker1Unique=~Biomarker1
Biomarker2Unique=~Biomarker2
Biomarker3Unique=~Biomarker3

Thank you!
Gabe

messages.author: ac421cf36d1a4c37
messages.subject: Re: Number of latent variables
parts:
Hi Gabe. That’s a standard common (+ unique) factor model. The unique factors don’t need to be specified though because they are equivalent to residual variances. If you do specify them you need to fix the residuals to 0.  
If you go onto add a snp effect you want be able to specify it on all 4 factors as it will be under identified. However the Q statistic can be used to test whether the snp effect on the common factor is sufficient to account for the patterning of SNP effects. 
Elliot

parts:
Hi Elliot,
Thank you!

Running a common factor model for the three traits and  ~ 1 million SNPs I get 1011 variants with lavaan warnings.
Most commonly I get: lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

And for a ~10 SNPs I get no output and:
lavaan WARNING: 

How do you typically handle such SNPS/errors?

Here is one example locus of interest where I get "estimated ov variances are negative” errors.
Surprisingly the Q_pval at this locus are not particularly low (for the index variant 10^-3). Can you help me understand what is happening here?

Thank you!
Gabe

<Image 5-4-21 at 9.39 PM.jpg>

On May 1, 2021, at 5:36 AM, Elliot Tucker-Drob <tucke...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Gabe,

We normally remove Q hits from our list of factor hits. A factor hit that is also a Q hit is likely a false discovery for the factor that is driven by effects on only a subset of the phenotypes loading on that factor. When pruning your list of factor hits for heterogeneity, you could use a genome wide threshold for Q or something more lax (eg a bonferroni correction for the number of factor loci). 

I recommend seeing what we’ve done in some of our recent work below. Don’t forget to check out the supplements!

Elliot

messages.author: ac421cf36d1a4c37
messages.subject: Re: Number of latent variables
parts:
Hi Gabe,

It's hard to say what's going on there without digging in a bit more. Below are some directions I'd recommend looking into.

I'd first verify that the loadings in your no snp model look OK (i.e. none greater than 1.0, none close to 0). You said the rGs are .3-.6, so it sounds like that's not an issue.

Given that this locus clearly has an effect on only 1 of the phenotypes, I suppose it is surprising that Q isn't more significant. However, if the Ns for Trait and Trait3 are much smaller than that for Trait2, this would explain things. It would also explain things if only trait 2 has a high loading on the factor (as the common pathways model implies that snps will have effects on the traits proportional to their loadings). In the case in which 2 out of 3 of your indicators have trivial loadings, there may not be much benefit to using the factor model in the first place.

I suggest checking the model estimates and checking for smooth warnings for the problematic SNPs. If there has not been excessive smoothing, you are confident that there isn't an error in the code, and the model estimates all look reasonable, then the warnings may be ignorable. If a small number of SNPs fail, that may be acceptable loss, especially if they are not SNPs with particularly significant univariate estimates and/or in loci in which many of the other SNPs have converged successfully.

You might consider specifying this model using the usergwas function and constraining the residual variances of the indicators and the factor to be nonnegative.

Finally, it looks like the locus zoom plots probably have -log(p) on the y axis.. If so, the -logp values are extremely high for Trait 2. Are you sure this a polygenic trait? It may just be that the N is very large, but if it's not, then you may be talking about a locus with a very large effect. You said these are biomarkers, so it may have a core pathway and a polygenic background, e.g. as per the recent Sinnott-Armstrong  et al. paper (https://elifesciences.org/articles/58615). If so there may be some issues involved in estimating h2 and rg using LDSC on the traits and then incorporating effect sizes from an extremely large effect size locus. These are not insurmountable, but they would require a bit of care.

I hope these leads are helpful;

All the best,

Elliot
